open-question.question: Eight alternatives returns were refused as malformed XML in field runs, seven for a mismatched tag and one for a raw element such as `<Link>` written in an alternative's text, each costing its one repair; the agent's rendering rule names `&` and `<` as the characters to write as entities. Is this closed, by a change to the agent's rendering rule or to what the tool accepts, or only recorded as accepted?
open-question.recommendation: All eight refusals were recovered by the pass's one repair and a refused file never reaches the document, so no wrong state can result, and more rendering rules for a failure this rare would weigh on every agent's file.
open-question.alternative: Nothing changes in the agent's file, the corrective message, or the tool; CLAUDE.md records the entry as accepted, with its reason: eight refused returns in the field runs, each recovered by the pass's one repair, whose `Error:` line names the position that failed, and a question whose repair is refused again left bare by the closing `list --without-alternatives` for the next run. The existing repair already absorbs the failure at the cost of one turn per affected question, and a refused file never reaches the document, so no wrong state can result and no tool, contract, or prose surface grows. Every such refusal keeps costing a repair round, and a second malformation in the repair leaves the question without alternatives until another pass runs, a delay an unattended chain meets as a skipped question.

Close it in the agent's file alone, with the open-question tool unchanged. Step 3's rendering rule names the forms that broke: every `<` that does not open or close one of the three element tags is written `<`, placeholders such as `<path>` or `<MISSION_DIR>` and element names quoted as text such as `<Link>` included, every bare `&` is written `&`, and the sentence saying escaping is not the agent's to get right is cut. Step 4 gains a third mechanical test beside its two: every `<` left raw in the draft opens or closes an `<alternative>`, `<advantage>`, or `<drawback>` tag, and every such tag is closed in order. The fixed corrective message and the one-repair cap stay as they are. CLAUDE.md records the outcome as a prose fix. It aims at the stated cause where it arises, in the one file the agent reads, with no tool contract, call, or turn added; the current rule's closing sentence ("indentation and escaping are not yours to get right") reads as permission not to escape, so removing it is a plain correction. The rule already named `&` and `<` when the eight refusals happened, so sharper wording and a by-eye test may not lower the rate, and since the change is prose only no test can pin it, so whether it closed anything is known only from later field runs.

The open-question tool gains a check-only form of `embed --alternatives` (a `--check` flag or a subcommand of its own) that runs the same extraction, fragment parse, and block validation against the named block and writes nothing, printing nothing on success and the same `Error:` line `embed` would print. The agent's step 4 runs it once on its `.xml.part` file before the `mv`, revises the draft against any `Error:` line and runs it again, so the agent's open-question calls become three rather than exactly two. The agent's rendering rule is otherwise unchanged, the orchestrator's batch call, repair, and skip are unchanged, and a test pins the check form's refusal of a raw `<Link>` and a mismatched tag with the document unchanged. It catches every malformation, the agent's own mismatched format tags as well as raw markup in text, inside the agent's session where its analysis is intact, using the tool's exact validation rather than a by-eye reading, so a refusal at the batch call should no longer occur and no repair round is spent. Every alternatives agent pays one more tool call on every run to save a repair that eight field returns needed, and it reverses the agent's "exactly two calls" contract and adds a form to the tool, a tested surface kept for good.

alternative.id: Tool reads stray markup as text

open-question.alternative: The open-question tool's fragment parser, shared by both `embed` forms, gains a pre-pass before the XML parse: a `<` that does not open or close one of the format's child tags is taken as a literal `<`, and an `&` that does not start an entity as a literal `&`, so a raw placeholder or `<Link>` in an alternative's text is embedded as text and rendered escaped in the canonical form. A genuinely mismatched format tag (an unclosed `<advantage>`, a `</drawback>` where `</advantage>` belongs) is still refused. The agent's file keeps its rule, or drops it as no longer needed, and tests pin the accepted text and the still-refused mismatch. It removes the failure for raw text markup mechanically, pinned by a test, with no added agent turn and no reliance on the agent obeying a rule it has already broken; the recommendation pass's hand-rendered fragments gain the same tolerance. The tool stops being a strict XML reader and carries a second grammar of its own deciding what a `<` means, which is the kind of guessing the tools otherwise refuse, and it cannot help where the seven "mismatched tag" refusals were format tags the agent itself mis-nested rather than raw text, which the field counts do not separate.

The agent's rendering rule changes the format it writes: each what-it-is text and each `<advantage>` and `<drawback>` text is written inside a `<![CDATA[ … ]]>` section, so nothing inside it is escaped by hand and a raw `<` or `&` is text; the tool is unchanged, since its parser already reads CDATA as text and its canonical render writes the result escaped. The step 4 tests gain one: no field text holds `]]>`. It replaces a rule the agent must apply character by character with one fixed wrapper per field, so placeholders and quoted element names, the commonest content of this project's alternatives, need no escaping at all, with no tool change. It is a new authoring form only the agent's prose carries, which the agent can forget or apply to some fields and not others, leaving the same refusal, it does nothing for mis-nested format tags, and being prose only it is pinned by no test.

open-question.question: The commit tool repeats every git write that exits 128, up to 16 attempts over about four seconds, reading only the exit status and never git's message, so a failure no lock caused, such as a pathspec matching no file, is repeated to the last attempt before its error prints. Does the tool keep repeating every exit 128, or does it stop at once on one no lock caused, which needs it to read git's message text or to tell the two cases apart some other way?
open-question.recommendation: No lock is ever missed over git's wording or locale, and the cost is about four seconds before a failure that ends the call anyway, with git's own message still printed whole.
open-question.alternative: The commit tool keeps repeating every git write that exits 128 on the present schedule (16 attempts, 0.25 seconds apart), reading only the exit status and no message text. A failure no lock caused, such as `git add` of a pathspec matching no file, is still repeated to the last attempt before its `Error:` line prints. The committing invariant stays as written, and CLAUDE.md records the entry as accepted with its reason. Nothing changes in the tool, its tests, or the committing invariant, and no lock is ever missed because of git's wording, its locale, or a new lock message: the only cost is about four seconds before a failure that ends the call anyway, and git's own message still reaches the runner whole. Every non-lock 128 costs about four seconds and reports itself as "on all 16 attempts", which reads as a held lock and can send a runner to look for one; how often this happens depends on how the sibling question on committing a removed path settles, since that case is the one reproduced.

The tool keeps repeating every exit 128 without reading any message, but its one schedule constant is cut to a smaller window (for example a handful of attempts over about one second), so a non-lock failure surfaces sooner; nothing tells the two kinds of failure apart. The change is two constants and the retry test's bounds, with no message parsing and no new branch, and it shrinks the wasted wait on every non-lock failure in proportion. It narrows the window that absorbs another run's ordinary write, the reason the retry exists, below the bounds `tests/test_commit_retry.py` pins as decided, so concurrent runs (two completion runs, a sweep beside a completion run) collide more often; and a non-lock failure is still repeated and still reported as a multi-attempt failure.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads git's stderr and repeats the write only when it holds git's lock-file text (the `Unable to create '….lock': File exists` form that a held index, `HEAD`, or ref lock prints); every other exit 128 is passed on at once as one `Error:` line after its single attempt. Git is run with a fixed C locale so the message is not translated. The committing invariant's "no message text is read" is revised and the retry tests gain a non-lock 128 that fails on the first attempt. It stops exactly the failures that are not locks, whatever their cause, so a pathspec, repository, or permission failure is reported at once and honestly as one attempt, while every lock git reports in its standard form is still absorbed. The tool depends on git's message wording: a git version that rewords the lock message, or a lock failure printed in another form, is no longer retried and collides at once, the failure the retry was built to prevent; the fixed locale must cover every git write the tool runs.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads git's stderr and stops at once only when it matches a short stated list of failures no lock causes (starting with `pathspec '…' did not match any files`); every other exit 128, an unrecognized message included, is repeated on the present schedule. Git runs under a fixed C locale; the committing invariant is revised to name the list. A wording change in git or an unlisted message falls back to today's behaviour, so no lock is ever left unretried; the reproduced case and any later one found in the field stop at once. It closes only the failures someone has listed, so each new non-lock 128 still waits the full window until it is added, and the list is message-matching code the tool must keep current with git; if the sibling question on removed paths stops the pathspec case from reaching git, the list may hold nothing that occurs.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads no message text but checks git's own lock files, resolved through `git rev-parse --git-path` (the index lock, `HEAD.lock`, and the current branch's ref lock): it repeats the write while one of them exists, repeats it once more when none exists so a lock released between the failure and the probe is still absorbed, and passes on a further 128 with no lock file present after that second attempt. It tells a lock from a non-lock by the lock itself rather than by git's wording or locale, so the invariant's "no message text is read" can stand, and a non-lock failure ends after two attempts instead of sixteen. The tool gains file probes and a branch on what git keeps under its directory, a lock it does not probe (another ref, a packed-refs or config lock) is treated as a non-lock after two attempts, and the retry test must hold each probed lock file, so the mechanics grow more than a message match would.
